title: Razor Syntax Fundamentals
description: Master the basic Razor syntax for mixing C# code and HTML to build dynamic web pages.

blocks.text: Razor is a templating engine that lets you write C# code directly inside HTML files. The result is a Razor view or page that can generate dynamic HTML based on data from your controller or page model.

Razor files use the .cshtml extension. The @ symbol is the gateway between HTML and C#. Anything after @ is treated as C# until the parser reaches an HTML element again. This makes Razor feel natural if you already know HTML.

blocks.title: Razor Is Not a Language
blocks.text: Razor is a syntax that the ASP.NET Core runtime translates into a C# class. The generated class inherits from a base page type and writes HTML to the response stream. You rarely need to think about this translation, but it helps to know it exists.

The simplest Razor construct is the code expression. It evaluates a C# expression and writes the result into the HTML output. You use @ followed by a C# expression. The framework automatically HTML-encodes the output to prevent injection attacks.

blocks.title: Code Expressions in Razor
blocks.content: Use @ to output values and run simple expressions.

blocks.text: Notice the @( ... ) syntax in the last two lines. When you need to mix C# expressions with punctuation that Razor might confuse for HTML, wrap the expression in parentheses.

A code block lets you write multiple C# statements. You start with @{ and close with }. The code inside runs before the HTML is rendered. Use code blocks to declare variables, call methods, or perform calculations.
Code blocks do not write output directly unless you call a method like WriteLiteral or Write. The variables and logic you define inside a code block are available to the rest of the page.

blocks.title: Loops and Conditions in Razor
blocks.content: Use standard C# control structures inside Razor.

blocks.text: Razor pages and views usually receive a Model object from the framework. You access it directly in the view using the Model property. The @model directive at the top of the file tells Razor what type to expect, which enables IntelliSense and compile-time checking.

blocks.title: Strongly Typed Razor Page
blocks.content: Declare the model type at the top of the .cshtml file.

blocks.title: Razor Syntax Quick Reference
items: @Model.Property - Reads a property from the page model or view model.
@{ ... } - Code block for multiple C# statements.
@foreach (var item in items) { ... } - Loop over a collection.
@using Namespace - Imports a namespace for the rest of the page.
@inject IService Service - Injects a service into the view.
@functions { ... } - Defines helper methods or properties on the generated class.

terms.definition: The combination of @ symbols and C# code that allows dynamic content inside HTML files.
A single C# expression prefixed with @ that evaluates and writes its result into the HTML.
A section wrapped in @{ ... } containing multiple C# statements that run before rendering.
A declaration at the top of a Razor file that specifies the expected type of the Model property.
The automatic conversion of special characters to safe HTML entities, preventing script injection.

blocks.title: Exercise: Build a Product List Page
blocks.description: Create a Razor Page that displays a list of products with prices and a total.
steps: Create a Products Razor Page with a ProductsModel that supplies a list of Product objects.
Declare @model List<Product> at the top of the .cshtml file.
Use a @foreach loop to render each product in an HTML table.
Format prices as currency using ToString("C").
Calculate the total price using a code block and display it below the table.
Add an @if block that shows a message when the total exceeds 500.
blocks.expectedOutcome: You will have a page that dynamically renders a table of products and a total price using Razor syntax.

items.text: I can explain what the @ symbol does in a Razor file.
items.hint: It switches from HTML into C# code.

items.text: I know the difference between a code expression and a code block.
items.hint: Expression returns a value; block runs statements.

items.text: I can use @model to make a view strongly typed.
items.hint: Place @model ProductList at the top of the file.

items.text: I can write a foreach loop and an if statement inside Razor.
items.hint: Standard C# syntax works inside @{ ... } or inline with @.

blocks.title: Summary
points: Razor mixes C# and HTML using the @ symbol.
Code expressions output a single value; code blocks run multiple statements.
The @model directive gives your view a strongly typed Model property.
Razor automatically HTML-encodes output to prevent injection attacks.
Standard C# control structures like if, foreach, and switch work in Razor.
blocks.takeaway: Razor syntax is intentionally lightweight. Once you know where @ transitions to C#, you can write any logic you need inside a view while keeping the HTML readable.
